title: Greenfield Savings - Data residency & compliance discovery
summary: Discovery focused on data residency needs for financial workloads. Customer currently uses managed cloud in us-east and wants options for in-region hosting and stricter logging controls for PCI/HIPAA-like workflows. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, KMS/HSM key management, audit logs retention and redaction, SOC2/ISO evidence, and steps to run a pilot and red-team style review.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Compliance: GDPR, SOC2, HIPAA, PCI-like controls
Next steps: pilot and security pack
action_items: Alex Chen: Send Redwood security pack (SOC2 report, ISO certs, GDPR whitepaper) - due 2026-10-18
Priya Das: Provide sample network diagram for Private/VPC deployment and list of required ports - due 2026-10-20
Michael Ortega / Greenfield: Share list of regulated workloads and PII data flows (high level) - due 2026-10-21
next_steps: Redwood to send compliance artifacts and architecture diagram
Schedule a 1-hour technical deep dive (SE-led) for 2026-10-22
Customer to identify pilot application and timeframe (2-4 week pilot suggested)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14 14:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Michael (CISO - Greenfield), Sara (Head Cloud Ops), David (VP Product), Lena (Compliance)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Alex Chen from Redwood, account exec. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Jordan might pop in later. How's everybody doing?
[00:08] Michael: Doing good, Alex. Thanks. Michael Ortega here, CISO for Greenfield Savings. We've got Sara, David and Lena on. Quick note we're trying to keep this to compliance & residency questions today.
[00:18] Alex: Totally, that's the plan. We'll run through high level Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options, answer questions on logs, KMS, residency and then Priya will jump into some technical details.
[00:27] Sara: Great. We're trying to understand whether Redwood Hosted can meet our requirements or if we need Dedicated or Private deployment. Our main constraints are OFAC/regulatory data residency in us-east-1 and tighter logging controls for some PCI-like services.
[00:40] Priya: Thanks, Sara. Quick clarifier - when you say residency do you mean strict region-bound processing (no egress to other regions) and also data at rest restricted to customer keys?
[00:50] Lena: Exactly. We need proof of data never leaving the US and encryption keys we control; ideally HSM-backed. Also we need to reduce what gets logged - e.g., redact PII from request/response logs, and limit audit log retention to our policy.
[01:05] David: And we have an internal timeline - pilot in Q4, production mid Q1. We're in a procurement window and evaluating a couple of vendors.
[01:14] Alex: Helpful. High level - Redwood Hosted (our standard API) is multi-region and can be configured to process in-region, but for customers with strict key control and non-egress guarantees we usually recommend Redwood Dedicated or Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). Dedicated gives you reserved capacity in a region and better isolation; Private puts the control plane closer to your network and supports customer-managed KMS/HSM.
[01:33] Michael: Can you explain the differences in terms of logs? We can't have full request/response logs retained by vendors for some workloads.
[01:41] Priya: Absolutely. On Hosted we do capture request metadata and we offer optional request/response logging which is off by default for customers with sensitive data. For Dedicated, logs are still collected by Redwood's control plane but we support filtering and faster deletion windows. For Private, logs can be routed to your logging stack - e.g., Splunk or S3 in your VPC - and you control retention and redaction before they leave your network.
[02:05] Sara: So Private would let us avoid Redwood storing raw responses entirely?
[02:09] Priya: Yes, in a Private deployment you can configure no-logs policies and have the audit trail stay in your environment. If you want absolute proof, we also support a mode where request bodies aren't persisted - only telemetry counters - but that has tradeoffs for debugging.
[02:22] Michael: What about KMS? We run AWS KMS with CloudHSM for our HSM-backed keys. Need to ensure keys never leave our account.
[02:30] Priya: We support customer-managed keys via KMS integration in Dedicated and Private. For Hosted, we offer envelope encryption where you can bring your own key (BYOK) but some customers prefer Dedicated/Private to plug their KMS directly into the runtime. Note: some of the terminology in our docs gets transcribed as "Redwood Dedictaed" in older notes - apologies for that, it's Dedicated.
[02:48] Alex: Quick add - for high assurance we can do an HSM integration and we have an enterprise onboarding checklist that lists the KMS/HSM patterns we support.
[02:56] David: On GDPR - while we're US-based, some of our customers are EU residents. We need to understand data subject requests and the ability to delete data on demand. How does Redwood support that?
[03:06] Priya: Good question. We provide tooling for data subject access and deletion for data processed in Redwood Hosted within EU regions. For Dedicated/Private where you control data stores, it's usually modeled into your retention policies. If you keep logs in your S3, you can implement deletion flows that meet GDPR. We also provide support materials and assistance during audits.
[03:22] Lena: We also need SOC2 and ISO attestation for vendor risk. Do you have recent reports?
[03:27] Alex: Yes - we have a SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001. I'll send the redacted report after the call. That should cover the baseline.
[03:34] Michael: Good. One more technical: does Redwood store any partial context in a remote cache or default KV store that could cause data to replicate outside region?
[03:43] Priya: The runtime uses KV cache for generation performance. In Hosted, that cache is region-bound but we have cross-region failover capability. For strict residency you'd disable cross-region failover and pin to region, or use Dedicated/Private where the KV is in your network. There's also a config to avoid persisting cache to long-term storage.
[04:03] Sara: Are there any limitations with Private for our expected throughput? We have bursty daily peaks during statement generation and need predictable latency.
[04:12] Priya: Dedicated is usually the sweet spot for predictable throughput because you get reserved GPU pools. Private can also be sized but comes with more ops overhead. If you want minimal ops and predictable SLA, Dedicated in your region is a common choice for banks - you still get strong controls and you can combine with customer-managed KMS in some patterns.
[04:30] Michael: About logging restrictions - can Redwood redact PII automatically before logs? Like names, account numbers.
[04:36] Priya: We have redaction templates and a PII detection pipeline that can mask or drop tokens before logs are stored. On Hosted we can apply that at ingestion; on Private you can run your own redaction. There are edge cases where model outputs recreate PII so we recommend prompt engineering + redaction.
[04:52] Alex: Also worth noting we support per-route policies so you can have stricter handling for routes that process regulated data and a more permissive policy for general-purpose routes.
[04:59] David: Thanks. Any discussion on legal process - e.g., if regulators request logs, what's the process?
[05:05] Alex: We have a vendor legal escalation path and we comply with lawful requests; for Private deployments where logs live in your environment, Redwood's involvement is limited. We can work with your legal team and we also provide assistance for audit evidence.
[05:18] Michael: Do you support SSO (SAML) and IAM/role mapping for RBAC?
[05:22] Priya: Yes, SSO via SAML/OIDC, SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC with fine-grained roles. Those features are available across Hosted and Dedicated; for Private you can sync with your IdPs inside the VPC.
[05:34] Sara: Are there known gotchas with PCI-type workloads? We're not sure if our payment flow requires PCI Level 1 vendor status but we need to ensure logs are handled as if they were PCI sensitive.
[05:44] Priya: We don't hold PCI certification specifically; customers often architect around that by keeping card data out of prompts and using tokenization. For flows that unavoidably touch cardholder data, Private or Dedicated with strict no-logs and on-prem routing is the recommended path. We'll share a patterns doc.
[05:59] Michael: Ok. Can you outline a suggested pilot architecture? Minimal scope: a single microservice that makes inference calls for customer support summarization that may contain PII.
[06:09] Priya: Sure. Suggested pilot: run on Dedicated in us-east with reserved capacity to avoid cross-region failover; integrate AWS KMS BYOK with HSM-backed keys; set request/response logging off, enable PII redaction at ingestion, retain only telemetry; send events to customer's S3 for audit copies; run a 2-week load test. We'll draft a diagram.
[06:28] Alex: We'll also propose success criteria: latency under 300ms p95 for summary endpoint, no logs retained with PII, and a security review signoff from your team.
[06:36] David: That's reasonable. Pricing question - Dedicated vs Hosted delta?
[06:41] Alex: Dedicated is typically committed capacity with a monthly/annual reserve; cost is higher but more predictable. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll send ballpark numbers after the call - depends heavily on tokens and concurrency.
[06:52] [10:02] (brief silence while folks check docs)
[10:10] Michael: A couple nitty-gritty items: are you able to provide network diagrams for Private VPC peering and required egress ports?
[10:18] Priya: Yes, Priya here - I'll attach a sample network diagram and the port list. For Private there's a lightweight control plane that speaks over a set of known ports; the runtime nodes can live in your VPC. I'll also include a matrix of supported KMS options (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, on-prem HSM via PKCS11).
[10:36] Lena: For audit, can you provide log hashes or tamper-evidence if Redwood holds logs? We need chain-of-custody assurances.
[10:44] Alex: We can provide tamper-evident logs via cryptographic hashing and chain-of-custody metadata for hosted logs - and for Dedicated we have configuration to rotate and deliver logs to your archive daily. For Private, you own the archive.
[10:58] Sara: Any mention of cross-region failover - if there is an outage in us-east, can Redwood spin up in another region temporarily? That may violate our residency rules.
[11:07] Priya: By default we have failover, but for your use-case we'd disable auto failover and instead rely on capacity in-region; if you want DR we'll discuss an explicit failover plan and approvals.
[11:18] Michael: Are there customers in our sector doing this? Any references?
[11:22] Alex: We have smaller regional banks and a couple of fintechs on Dedicated with similar controls. I'll share anonymized references and a short case study.
[11:30] David: Good. On the technical deep dive - we'd like Priya to walk our infra team through runtime behavior: KV cache, how prompt context is paged, model quantization impacts, and latency tradeoffs.
[11:41] Priya: Happy to. We'll book a 60-90 minute SE-led session and include some perf slides and an offline benchmark spreadsheet. Note: some of the model names in our catalog are abbreviated in docs; don't rely on the short names.
[11:54] Alex: Quick recap and owner notes. Action items: I'll send SOC2/ISO and pricing; Priya will send network diagram and KMS matrix; Michael will surface pilot app and PII flows. We'll aim to lock pilot scope in one week.
[12:08] Michael: Sounds good. Any last security red flags you see?
[12:12] Priya: No red flags, just typical things - keep card data outside prompts, pin region, use BYOK/HSM, and set strict logging policies. Also consider rate-limiting and quota for the pilot.
[12:23] Sara: Thanks, that's helpful.
[12:26] Alex: Great - we'll follow up with the pack. Thanks everyone.
[12:29] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "Redwood Dedicated" transcribed in earlier notes as "Redwood Dedictaed"; "HSM" sometimes as "H M S"; some acronyms spelled out intermittently.
